query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles remain structurally and chemically stable during prolonged heating to 773–1173 K in catalytic and 473–1923 K in thermoelectric environments because short-range compositional fluctuations, enhanced by in-situ formed protective interfacial layers, inhibit large-scale element segregation and prevent coarsening.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with low noble-metal content, supported on a suitable substrate (e.g., carbon).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary temperature (up to 1173 K for catalytic, up to 1923 K for thermoelectric) and gaseous environment (oxidizing and reducing gas compositions) in side-by-side microscopy chambers to compare (i) as-prepared nanoparticles versus (ii) identical nanoparticles intentionally doped at low levels (e.g., ∼1–2 at%) with a heavier element that promotes short-range ordering.
generation.conditions: Perform in-situ transmission electron microscopy and atomistic simulations under the catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) operating atmospheres to track nanoparticle morphology, compositional distribution, and phase evolution in real time.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range compositional ordering that acts as a diffusion barrier to large-scale phase separation or core–shell segregation, aided by protective surface oxide or carbon-based interfacial layers forming at elevated temperatures.
generation.mechanism: When a small fraction of a heavier dopant is present in the near-equiatomic nanoparticles, the resulting local compositional perturbations promote self-limiting diffusion pathways and stable, coherent interfaces. These effects collectively hinder the onset of coarsening and chemical phase separation under prolonged high-temperature operation in reactive atmospheres.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to undoped control nanoparticles, the doped multi-element nanoparticles exhibit smaller changes in particle size, composition, or morphology; their stable single-phase character remains largely unchanged even after extended exposure to target service temperatures and redox conditions.
generation.baseline: Similarly prepared but undoped near-equiatomic nanoparticles exposed to the same environment show more pronounced coarsening, phase separation, or segregation over the same time scale.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis holds if the doping fraction remains within ranges that maintain solid-solution behavior (i.e., below solubility limits) and if operating temperatures and redox potentials do not exceed the thresholds for dissolution of the protective surface phase.
generation.uncertainty: Interfacial chemistry with specific supports or highly oxidizing environments may influence multiphase formation, thus further refinements of the doping level or alternative stable-phase compositions could be required.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct simultaneous in-situ heating experiments in an aberration-corrected TEM with matched pairs of nanoparticles, one set with the dopant and one without. Track their structural and compositional evolution at intervals up to 1923 K, correlating real-time images with post-mortem high-resolution microscopy and chemical analysis.
measurements: Particle size distributions before and after testing, measured via electron microscopy.
Local compositional maps (e.g., via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and/or atom probe tomography).
Phase identification by in-situ electron diffraction or X-ray diffraction.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If doped nanoparticles exhibit the same degree of coarsening or compositional segregation as undoped nanoparticles, or if no stable surface phase forms to suppress grain growth, then the proposed mechanism of short-range ordering and protective layer formation is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Properties such as standard reduction potential (E0), cohesive energy density (CED),, and atomic radius aid in delineating the propensity and feasibility of the oxidation reaction. Thermodynamically, elements with the closest and deepest local minima act spontaneously given favorable conditions. AbstractDirect formation of ultra-small nanoparticles on carbon supports by rapid high temperature synthesis method offers new opportunities for scalable nanomanufacturing and the synthesis of stable multi-elemental nanoparticles. However, the underlying mechanisms affecting the dispersion and stability of nanoparticles on the supports during high temperature processing remain enigmatic. In this work, we report the observation of metallic nanoparticles formation and stabilization on carbon supports through in situ Joule heating method. We find that the formation of metallic nanoparticles is associated with the simultaneous phase transition of amorphous carbon to a highly defective turbostratic graphite (T-graphite). Molecular dynamic (MD) simulations suggest that the defective T-graphite provide numerous nucleation sites for the nanoparticles to form. Furthermore, the nanoparticles partially intercalate and take root on edge planes, leading to high binding energy on support. This interaction between nanoparticles and T-graphite substrate strengthens the anchoring and provides excellent thermal stability to the nanoparticles.
